extracted.intended_audience: British political public, lawmakers, and readers of 18th-century political philosophy (general educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: A rhetorical and legal-philosophical argument about the legitimate bases of sovereignty in Britain, defending hereditary succession and established constitutional mechanisms against revolutionary doctrines that tie legitimacy to popular election or facile deposition. The text lays out standards for when change is justified and how constitutional continuity should be preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawful sovereignty tied to popular choice (revolutionary doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that 'his Majesty is almost the only lawful king in the world, because the only one who owes his crown to the choice of his people'—i.e. that a sovereign is lawful only if raised by popular election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke treats this as either nonsense or a dangerous, illegal, and unconstitutional principle. He warns it would render all other monarchs 'usurpers' and would slowly habituate public opinion to an abstract principle that could later be used to undermine existing government. Anti-pattern: accepting the abstract doctrine without examining its concrete implications; allowing pulpit eloquence to 'pickle' the theory for future use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolution Society's three claimed rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The society asserts that, by the principles of the Revolution, the people of England have acquired three fundamental rights: (1) 'To choose our own governors.' (2) 'To cashier them for misconduct.' (3) 'To frame a government for ourselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke presents these three as the core revolutionary claims and systematically rejects them as belonging to a faction, not the body of the people. He argues the body of the people disclaim them, will resist their practical assertion, and that these claims are not grounded in the Declaration of Right or subsequent settlement acts. Each claim is examined individually elsewhere in the text for its consequences and mischief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of Right as corner-stone: rights and succession inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Declaration of Right (1 Will. & Mary, sess. 2, ch. 2) declares 'the rights and liberties of the subject, and for settling the succession of the crown,' binding rights and succession together rather than recognizing a general right to choose governors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Declaration of Right as the authoritative constitutional standard: it contains no suggestion of a general right to elect sovereigns. Burke advises to consult the statute acts (Declaration of Right; 12th & 13th Will.) to determine constitutional principles instead of abstract revolutionary rhetoric. Anti-pattern: reading revolutionary maxims into these statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize from exceptional acts (privilegium non transit in exemplum)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deviation in one special case (e.g., the temporary settlement at the Revolution) does not provide a precedent to establish a general principle (i.e., making elective succession the rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal principle: do not draw a universal rule from a law enacted in a special circumstance. Burke points out Parliament's action in 1688 was an act of necessity and designed to preserve continuity; it was not intended to found an elective principle. Anti-pattern: treating exceptional solutions as general constitutional doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession as guarantor of unity, peace, and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The settled hereditary succession (as established and reinforced by statute) preserves 'unity, peace, and tranquillity' and is a pledge of stability for the rest of the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that hereditary succession has historically preserved liberties and institutional continuity; even when deviations occurred, the legislature sought to maintain the inheritable principle. He treats hereditary succession as a practical security for liberty, not an indefeasible divine right. Use historical practice and statute to justify hereditary succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on the meaning of 'misconduct' as ground for deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim to 'cashier' governors for mere 'misconduct' is too loose and indefinite to support deposition: the Revolution leaders grounded their action on grave, concrete illegal acts and a design to subvert Church, State, and fundamental laws, not on vague misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard for lawful removal: requires grave and demonstrable violations (e.g., attempts to subvert Protestant Church and State, a multitude of illegal overt acts) and not ambiguous, catch-all notions of misconduct. Anti-patterns: using broad labels like 'misconduct' to justify political overthrow; confusing popular indignation with constitutional grounds for deposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional remedies preferred over popular deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The state secured liberty and checked executive vice through statutes: making ministers responsible, frequent parliaments, impeachment, and legal provisions preventing royal pardon from invalidating impeachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke urges reliance on institutional and parliamentary mechanisms (inspection by representatives, impeachment, limitation of pardons) as safer and more constitutional means to check abuses than inventing a right to depose sovereigns by popular fiat. Use existing legal processes rather than revolutionary methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral competence vs. abstract sovereign power — limits on renunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: While abstract sovereign power may be unlimited in theory, there are moral limits: constituent parts of the state (House of Lords, House of Commons) are not morally competent to abdicate or renounce their constitutional functions or dissolve themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constituent bodies are bound by public faith and must preserve their portions of the constitution. Burke emphasizes that moral competence subjects even sovereign acts to reason, faith, justice, and fixed fundamental policy. Anti-pattern: claiming absolute ability to renounce institutional obligations under the name of 'sovereignty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Conserve and correct — change confined to defective parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A state without means to change is unfit to conserve itself; yet change should be confined to the 'peccant part' only, effected without decomposing the whole civil order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle for constitutional reform: repair or regenerate the impaired parts through the unaffected parts of the constitution (preserve continuity). Avoid wholesale reconstruction of society from first elements. Practical guidance: accept occasional, narrowly targeted amendments rather than revolutionary re-foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory settlement binding future succession for security
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament's acts (e.g., 12 & 13 Will.) can lawfully bind 'us, and our heirs, and our posterity' to a line of succession (Protestant succession) as a measure for the peace, quiet, and security of the realm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statute law to create certainty in succession where necessary for state security; such settlements were deliberate acts to secure liberties and prevent future dangerous choice. Example: naming Princess Sophia as the stock of inheritance to connect the Hanoverian line with James I's stock for continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the notion that the king is merely a 'servant' responsible to the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The new revolutionary phrasing that 'the king is no more than the first servant of the public, created by it, and responsible to it' is inconsistent with the British constitutional understanding that the monarch is 'our sovereign lord the king.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke cautions against the rhetorical adoption of 'servant' language: under British law the king is sovereign and obedience is owed to the law in him. The text argues that calling the king a servant misrepresents constitutional reality and may encourage unstable notions of removable sovereignty. Anti-pattern: flattering or insulting monarchy by rebranding it with populist labels that obscure legal status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposition by force is tantamount to war and destructive of law
rubrics_metrics.description: The ceremony of cashiering kings generally requires force and then 'becomes a case of war, and not of constitution': laws and tribunals fall silent amongst arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical injunction: avoid forcible deposing; recognise that resorting to force undermines legal institutions and constitutional order. Where force is used, constitutional remedies are supplanted by violence and chaos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical restraint: avoid using pulpit authority to propagate revolutionary doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Preachers (new evangelists) should keep bounds in democratic and levelling principles expected from titled pulpits; mixing pulpit authority with political revolution risks unsettling national tranquility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns anti-patterns: clergy preaching abstract revolutionary maxims and mobilising congregations (even attempting to drill them like regiments) threaten public order. He advises restraint and cautions that pulpit eloquence can 'pickle' doctrines for later misuse; rhetorical persuasion from pulpits should not substitute for constitutional deliberation.
